issues.legal_issue: A plaint amendment that replaces the original case, withdraws a clear admission, and adversely affects the opposing party is not permissible.
material_facts: The plaintiff originally sought recovery of money on the basis that the sale deed had become void, relying on the obligation to restore an advantage received under a void agreement or contract.

The proposed amendment recast the plaintiff’s position to assert the sale deed as valid and to seek relief based on the defendants’ alleged unauthorized occupation of the building, including mandatory possession and injunctions.
The amendment was sought about four years after the suit was instituted and would introduce a materially different case while removing the original admission.
The trial court allowed the amendment, but the High Court set that order aside; the plaintiff appealed.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was properly refused. The appeal was dismissed with costs.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC gives courts discretion to allow amendments necessary to determine the real controversy, subject to just terms; after trial has commenced, its proviso also requires a finding that despite due diligence the matter could not have been raised earlier. The court must assess whether the amendment is imperative for effective adjudication, bona fide, likely to cause prejudice that cannot adequately be compensated, whether refusal would cause injustice or multiplicity of litigation, whether it fundamentally changes the nature and character of the case, and, as a general rule, whether a fresh suit on the amended claim would be time-barred. A plaint amendment that materially substitutes the cause of action or nature of the claim is treated more restrictively than an amendment to a written statement; a clear admission in a plaint cannot be displaced where doing so would prejudice the opposing party. The court relied, among other authorities, on Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Hnaung, AIR 1922 PC 249; Cropper v. Smith (1884) 29 Ch D 700; Usha Balashaheb Swami v. Kiran Appaso Swami, (2007) 5 SCC 602; Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, (1998) 1 SCC 278; Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetley, (2008) 7 SCC 85; Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co., (1976) 4 SCC 320; Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram, (1978) 2 SCC 91; Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, (1974) 2 SCC 393; and B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameshwaram Pillai, (2000) 1 SCC 712.

rule.if: plaint_amendment_appeal and amendment_changes_nature_of_claim and amendment_withdraws_clear_admission and amendment_adversely_affects_opponent

predicates.plaint_amendment_appeal: A party challenged on appeal a decision allowing an amendment to its plaint.
predicates.amendment_changes_nature_of_claim: The proposed amendment replaced the original basis and nature of the plaintiff’s claim with a materially different case and relief.
predicates.amendment_withdraws_clear_admission: The plaintiff sought to remove a clear admission made in the original plaint about the legal effect of the transaction.
predicates.amendment_adversely_affects_opponent: The proposed change would adversely affect the opposing parties’ rights by requiring them to meet the materially different case.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns permission to amend a plaint and the proposed change alters the claim, withdraws a clear admission, and adversely affects the opposing party, the amendment is refused.
